mainTopic: Overlapping oaths, the definition of שבועת שוא, and whether an oath follows the swearer's private meaning
overview: The amud opens by finishing a case of two overlapping oaths. A man swore not to eat ten, then swore not to eat nine. He ate nine and brought a קרבן. After that, the tenth is only a חצי שיעור, so it carries no new קרבן. Then a new משנה defines a שבועת שוא, an empty oath. It covers swearing against an obvious fact, swearing about something impossible, and swearing not to testify or not to keep a מצוה. Taken on purpose, it earns מלקות. Taken by mistake, there is no penalty. In the גמרא, עולא says a fact counts as obvious once three people know it. אביי and רבא explain the odd wording 'if I did not see a flying camel.' רבינא then asks whether an oath follows the swearer's private meaning. Two proofs are pushed away: the court's warning before an oath, and משה's warning to ישראל. The גמרא ends by showing why משה needed to say whose meaning the oath followed.

steps.title: Figs, then grapes: only a half-measure is left
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its parallel case. A man swore not to eat figs and grapes together, then swore not to eat figs. He ate figs and set aside a קרבן. If he then eats grapes alone, that is only a חצי שיעור of the first oath, and no קרבן is owed.
steps.simpleTranslation: He ate figs and set aside an offering. Afterward he ate grapes alone. The grapes are only a half-measure, and for a half-measure he does not owe an offering.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a model case it started just before this section, to show when a leftover piece of an oath does not bring a new קרבן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the figs are 'used up' by the קרבן for the second oath, the grapes alone are only part of what the first oath covered, which was figs and grapes together. Eating only part of what an oath covers is a חצי שיעור, and a חצי שיעור does not bring a קרבן.

keyTerms.meaning: A half-measure: less than the full amount needed to be liable

phrases.english: and he ate figs and set aside an offering,
and afterward he ate grapes by themselves —
the grapes are a half-measure,
and for a half-measure he is not liable to an offering.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a model case begun just before this section.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Parallel case showing the leftover part is only a חצי שיעור
steps.terutzMaskana: Once the figs are covered by a קרבן, the grapes alone are only a half-measure of the first oath, so no קרבן is owed.

steps.title: Applying the same logic to ten and nine
steps.stepSummary: Using the words הכא נמי, the גמרא applies the figs-and-grapes logic to a man who swore not to eat ten and then swore not to eat nine.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too: he said, 'I swear I will not eat ten,' and then said, 'I swear I will not eat nine.' He ate nine and set aside an offering, and later ate the tenth. The tenth is a half-measure, and he is not liable for a half-measure.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא takes the model case and maps it onto the case it was really discussing: the oaths about ten and nine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The nine he ate are covered by the קרבן for the second oath. The tenth item alone is only a small part of the first oath, which covered all ten. So it counts as a חצי שיעור, and no קרבן is owed for it.

keyTerms.meaning: Here too, the same applies here
And then he went back and said

steps.whatToRemember: An oath that overlaps with an earlier oath can leave the earlier oath with only a חצי שיעור. Once a קרבן covers the overlapping part, eating the leftover part does not bring a new קרבן.

phrases.english: Here too, for example where he said:
"An oath that I will not eat ten,"
and then said again: "An oath that I will not eat nine,"
and he ate nine and set aside an offering,
and afterward he ate the tenth;
the tenth is a half-measure,
and for a half-measure he is not liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the model case from step 1 to the case under discussion.
steps.terutzMaskana: The tenth item alone is a חצי שיעור of the first oath, so he is not liable to a קרבן for it.

steps.title: New משנה: what is a שבועת שוא? Swearing against known facts
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה asks what a שבועת שוא is. Its first answer is swearing that something everyone knows is false is true, such as calling a stone pillar gold.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: What is an oath in vain? One who swears to change something people know: he says a stone pillar is gold, a man is a woman, or a woman is a man.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה opens and starts defining the kind of oath called שבועת שוא. Its first kind is swearing against a fact that everyone knows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה starts by switching from oaths about future actions to a different kind of oath. An oath that contradicts something everyone can plainly see is empty and useless, so it uses the Name for nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: The משנה (start of a new משנה)
An oath taken in vain, an empty or useless oath
To change, or deny, what is known

phrases.english: MISHNA:
Which is an oath in vain?
One who swore to change what is known to people —

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר עַל הָעַמּוּד שֶׁל אֶבֶן שֶׁהוּא שֶׁל זָהָב,
phrases.english: he said about a stone pillar that it is made of gold,
or about a man that he is a woman,
or about a woman that she is a man;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה begins a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Swearing that something everyone knows is false is true counts as a שבועת שוא.

steps.title: Second kind: swearing about something impossible
steps.stepSummary: The second kind of שבועת שוא is swearing that you saw something impossible, like a flying camel or a snake as big as an olive-press beam.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who swore about something impossible: 'If I did not see a camel flying in the air,' or 'If I did not see a snake as big as the beam of an olive press.'
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds a second kind of empty oath: swearing about something that cannot happen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This differs from the first kind. Nobody can see the impossible event to disprove it, but it simply cannot be true. Either way, the oath is plainly false and empty.

keyTerms.meaning: The beam of an olive press

phrases.aramaic: נִשְׁבַּע עַל דָּבָר שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לוֹ –
phrases.english: One who swore about a thing that is impossible —
"If I did not see a camel flying in the air"

phrases.aramaic: וְ״אִם לֹא רָאִיתִי נָחָשׁ כְּקוֹרַת בֵּית הַבַּד״;
phrases.english: or "If I did not see a snake like the beam of an olive press";
phrases.notes: That beam was a huge, heavy log, so this means an impossibly giant snake.

steps.triggerLanguage: נִשְׁבַּע עַל דָּבָר שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second kind of שבועת שוא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Swearing about something impossible is a שבועת שוא.

steps.title: Witnesses who swear not to testify
steps.stepSummary: A person asks witnesses to come testify for him, and they swear they will not. This is listed as another kind of שבועת שוא.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to witnesses, 'Come and testify for me,' and they answered, 'We swear that we will not testify for you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a case where witnesses take an oath to avoid testifying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Witnesses are already obligated by the תורה to testify. Their oath tries to cancel that duty, so it cannot take effect, and that makes it an oath in vain. This leads straight into the next line about swearing to cancel a מצוה.

phrases.english: He said to witnesses: "Come and testify for me,"
and they answered: "An oath that we will not testify for you";

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a third case to the list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Witnesses who swear not to testify have taken a שבועת שוא.

steps.title: Swearing not to do a מצוה
steps.stepSummary: Swearing to cancel a מצוה is a שבועת שוא. Examples are swearing not to build a סוכה, not to take a לולב, or not to put on תפילין.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who swore to cancel a מצוה: not to make a sukka, not to take a lulav, or not to put on tefillin.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the category of swearing to cancel a מצוה, with three examples.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person is already bound by an oath from Sinai to keep the מצוות, so a new oath cannot release him from them. Because the oath can never take effect, it is empty.

keyTerms.meaning: To cancel a מצוה, to refrain from doing it
A סוכה, the booth for סוכות
The palm branch taken on סוכות

steps.confusionAlert: This is about swearing NOT to do a מצוה. That oath cannot take effect at all, which is why it is called 'in vain.' It is not a regular oath that he must then keep.

phrases.english: One who swore to cancel a מצוה —
not to make a sukka,

phrases.aramaic: וְשֶׁלֹּא לִיטּוֹל לוּלָב וְשֶׁלֹּא לְהַנִּיחַ תְּפִילִּין;
phrases.english: or not to take a lulav, or not to put on tefillin;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Names the broader category of cancelling a מצוה, which also fits the witnesses case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oath to refrain from a מצוה is a שבועת שוא.

steps.title: The punishment for a שבועת שוא
steps.stepSummary: The משנה sums up: all these are a שבועת שוא. Taking one on purpose earns מלקות. Taking one by mistake carries no penalty.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is an oath in vain: for doing it on purpose one gets lashes, and for doing it by mistake he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה closes its list and states the punishment for a שבועת שוא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Done on purpose, a שבועת שוא earns מלקות. Done by mistake, it brings no קרבן, which is different from some other false oaths. So the penalty applies only when the person knew what he was doing.
steps.whatToRemember: A שבועת שוא can be swearing against a known fact, swearing about the impossible, or swearing to avoid a duty or מצוה. On purpose, the punishment is מלקות. By mistake, there is no penalty.

phrases.english: This is an oath in vain,
for whose intentional violation one is liable to lashes,
and for its unintentional violation he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: זוֹ הִיא שְׁבוּעַת שָׁוְא, שֶׁחַיָּיבִין עַל זְדוֹנָהּ מַכּוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sums up the list and gives the punishment.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A שבועת שוא earns מלקות if done on purpose and carries no penalty if done by mistake.

steps.title: Two clashing oaths about one loaf
steps.stepSummary: Someone swears to eat a loaf, then swears not to eat it. The first is a שבועת ביטוי and the second is a שבועת שוא.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone said 'I swear I will eat this loaf' and then said 'I swear I will not eat it,' the first is a שבועת ביטוי and the second is a שבועת שוא.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives one more example of a שבועת שוא. This time it is a second oath that contradicts an oath the person already made.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first oath is a normal promise about the future, so it is a שבועת ביטוי. The second oath swears to do the opposite of what he is already bound to do. It cannot take effect, so it is an empty oath, a שבועת שוא.

keyTerms.meaning: An oath of speech: a personal promise to do, or not do, something
A vain, empty oath that has no real effect

phrases.english: "On my oath, I will eat this loaf,"
"On my oath, I will not eat it" –
the first is an oath of speech,
and the second is a vain oath.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָרִאשׁוֹנָה שְׁבוּעַת בִּיטּוּי, וְהַשְּׁנִיָּה שְׁבוּעַת שָׁוְא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a final case to the משנה's list of vain oaths.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An oath that contradicts an earlier oath is a שבועת שוא. The earlier oath stays a שבועת ביטוי.

steps.title: Either way, he breaks one oath
steps.stepSummary: If he eats the loaf, he is guilty for the vain oath. If he does not eat it, he broke the oath of speech.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he ate it, he broke the rule against a vain oath. If he did not eat it, he broke his oath of speech.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה spells out what happens next with the two loaf oaths. He is caught either way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he eats, he keeps the first oath, and the second oath stands as the empty one he is guilty for. If he does not eat, he broke the first oath, which was real. No choice leaves him free of guilt.
steps.whatToRemember: With two clashing oaths, the first is real (שבועת ביטוי) and the second is empty (שבועת שוא). He ends up guilty for one of them no matter what he does.

phrases.english: If he ate it – he violated a vain oath.

phrases.aramaic: לֹא אֲכָלָהּ – עָבַר עַל שְׁבוּעַת בִּיטּוּי.
phrases.english: If he did not eat it – he violated an oath of speech.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the result of the case set up in step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eating makes him guilty for the vain oath. Not eating makes him guilty of breaking the oath of speech.

steps.title: עולא: 'known to all' means known to three people
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens with עולא. A false oath about something 'everyone knows' counts only if at least three people know the fact.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: עולא said: This applies when the fact is known to three people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by explaining the משנה's first case from step 3, the stone pillar called gold. עולא tells us how widely known a fact must be.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said a שבועת שוא includes swearing that something obviously false is true. עולא sets the bar for 'obvious.' If three people know the truth, the oath is a vain oath.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmud's discussion of the משנה

phrases.english: GEMARA
Ulla said:
And that is when it is known to three people.
phrases.notes: This goes back to the first case in the משנה, swearing a stone pillar is gold.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר עוּלָּא: וְהוּא שֶׁנִּיכָּר לִשְׁלֹשָׁה בְּנֵי אָדָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the גמרא by going back to the first case of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A fact counts as known to all once three people know it.

steps.title: Why does the משנה say 'if I did not see'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the flying camel case. It asks why the משנה says 'if I did not see' and not 'I swear that I saw.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: one swore about something impossible, 'If I did not see a camel flying in the air.' It did not say 'an oath that I saw.' What does 'if I did not see' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the second case of the משנה from step 4 and points to its strange wording. It is setting up two answers that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'If I did not see' sounds like half a sentence: if I did not see it, then what? A normal oath would say 'I swear that I saw.' The גמרא wants to know what the משנה's wording means.
steps.confusionAlert: 'If I did not see' is not a denial that he saw it. It is the 'if' half of a sentence, and the other half is missing. That missing half is exactly what the גמרא is asking about.

phrases.aramaic: נִשְׁבַּע עַל דָּבָר שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לוֹ –
phrases.english: He swore about something impossible –
"If I did not see a camel flying in the air."
It does not say "an oath that I saw,"
so what is "if I did not see"?

steps.triggerLanguage: ״שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁרָאִיתִי״ לָא קָאָמַר, מַאי ״אִם לֹא רָאִיתִי״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the first case of the משנה to the second, the flying camel.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the conditional wording 'if I did not see' means in the משנה.

steps.title: אביי: read it as 'an oath that I saw'
steps.stepSummary: אביי changes the wording of the משנה so it reads 'an oath that I saw.'
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Teach it as 'an oath that I saw.'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives the first answer. He fixes the wording of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For אביי, the 'if' wording is just not exact. The case is really a plain oath, 'I swear that I saw a flying camel.' That oath is false and impossible, so it is a שבועת שוא.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
Teach: "An oath that I saw."
phrases.notes: אביי is changing the words of the משנה, not explaining them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question about the wording by changing the text.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The משנה should read 'an oath that I saw.'

steps.title: רבא: it is the end of a longer vow
steps.stepSummary: רבא keeps the wording. He says the man said, 'Let all the fruits in the world be forbidden to me if I did not see a flying camel.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: It is where he says, 'Let all the fruits in the world be forbidden to me if I did not see a camel flying in the air.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a second answer to the same question. Unlike אביי, he does not change the משנה's words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבא, 'if I did not see' is the second half of a full sentence. The first half is that all the fruits in the world should be forbidden to him. So the משנה's wording is correct as written.
steps.whatToRemember: אביי fixes the wording to 'an oath that I saw.' רבא keeps 'if I did not see' and fills in the missing first half: 'let all the fruits in the world be forbidden to me.'

phrases.english: Rava said:
It is where he says: "Let all the fruits in the world be forbidden to me,"

phrases.aramaic: אִם לֹא רָאִיתִי גָּמָל פּוֹרֵחַ בָּאֲוִיר״.
phrases.english: "if I did not see a camel flying in the air."

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: בְּאוֹמֵר ״יֵאָסְרוּ כׇּל פֵּירוֹת שֶׁבְּעוֹלָם עָלַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to the same question, without changing the text as אביי did.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The wording is the end of a longer sentence that forbids all the world's produce to him on that condition.

steps.title: Maybe he calls a big bird a 'camel'
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asks רב אשי whether the man who swore he saw a flying camel really means a big bird he privately calls 'camel', so his oath would be true by his own meaning.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רב אשי: Maybe this man saw a big bird and called it 'camel' in his own head. Then when he swore, he swore by his own meaning, and his oath was true.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא challenges the ruling that the flying-camel oath is a vain oath. He suggests that the man may have had his own private meaning for the word 'camel'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case only counts as a שבועת שוא if the oath is obviously false. If the man privately uses 'camel' to mean a big bird, then by his own meaning he told the truth. So the question is whether private meaning counts in an oath.

keyTerms.meaning: He gave it a name, he called it
By his own understanding, by his private meaning

steps.whyThisMatters: This question opens the central issue of this part of the sugya: does an oath follow the plain public meaning of the words, or the swearer's private meaning?

phrases.english: Ravina said to Rav Ashi:

phrases.aramaic: וְדִלְמָא הַאי גַּבְרָא צִיפּוֹרָא רַבָּא חֲזִי,
phrases.english: But perhaps this man saw a big bird,
and gave it the name "camel,"

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי קָא מִשְׁתְּבַע – אַדַּעְתֵּיהּ דִּידֵיהּ אִישְׁתְּבַע?
phrases.english: and when he swears, he swore by his own understanding?
phrases.notes: So by his own meaning he really did see a flying 'camel', and the oath would be true.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבִינָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי: וְדִלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the flying-camel case that was just explained by אביי and רבא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that 'I saw a flying camel' is clearly a false, vain oath.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the swearer privately calls a big bird 'camel', his oath is true by his own meaning, so it might not be a vain oath.

steps.title: Proof from the court's warning before an oath
steps.stepSummary: רבינא backs up his challenge. A ברייתא says בית דין warns the swearer that he swears by the court's meaning, which suggests that private meaning would otherwise count.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say we go by what his mouth says and not by what he has in mind, a ברייתא teaches otherwise. When the court makes someone swear, they tell him: 'Know that we make you swear by our meaning and the court's meaning, not by yours.' Why do they say this? Isn't it because maybe he gave the lender worthless tokens and privately calls them 'zuzim', so he would swear by his own meaning?
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא blocks an easy answer, that we only follow the plain words. He brings a ברייתא to prove that private meaning can matter in an oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If only the plain words counted, בית דין would not need to warn anyone. The warning seems needed because a person could swear 'I paid you zuzim' while privately meaning tokens. That suggests that without the warning, his private meaning would count.

keyTerms.meaning: We follow his mouth, meaning the plain words he said
Following his mind, his private intention
According to the understanding of the court

phrases.english: And if you would say: we go after his mouth,
phrases.notes: Meaning we judge the oath by the plain meaning of the words he said.

phrases.english: and we do not go after his mind —

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא תַּנְיָא: כְּשֶׁמַּשְׁבִּיעִין אוֹתוֹ אוֹמְרִים לוֹ:
phrases.english: but isn't it taught: When they make him swear, they say to him:

phrases.aramaic: ״הֱוֵי יוֹדֵעַ, שֶׁלֹּא עַל דַּעְתְּךָ אָנוּ מַשְׁבִּיעִין אוֹתְךָ,
phrases.english: "Know that it is not by your understanding that we make you swear,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא עַל דַּעְתֵּנוּ וְעַל דַּעַת בֵּית דִּין״.
phrases.english: but by our understanding and by the understanding of the court."
What is the reason?
Is it not because we say:
perhaps he gave him tokens
and he calls them "zuzim,"

phrases.aramaic: דְּכִי קָא מִשְׁתְּבַע – אַדַּעְתֵּיהּ דִּידֵיהּ קָא מִשְׁתְּבַע?
phrases.english: so that when he swears, he swears by his own understanding?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבינא's challenge by blocking the answer that only the plain words count.
steps.raayaObject: That an oath can follow the swearer's private meaning.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about the warning בית דין gives before an oath.

steps.title: No, the warning is about רבא's cane trick
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that the court's warning is not about private meanings. It is aimed at the trick from רבא's court with the hollow cane.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. There, the court warns him because of the cane story in רבא's court.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי pushes away רבינא's proof. He gives a different reason for why the court warns the swearer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the cane story, a man hid the money he owed inside a cane, gave the cane to the lender to hold, and then swore he had 'given' him the money. His words were technically true, but it was a trick. The warning stops tricks like that, so it does not prove that private meanings of words count.

keyTerms.meaning: The cane of רבא, a famous trick that happened in רבא's court

steps.confusionAlert: The cane trick is different from the tokens case. In the cane case the words are literally true but the truth is hidden by a trick. In the tokens case a word is given a private meaning. רב אשי says the warning is only needed for tricks like the cane.

phrases.english: No, there it is because of the cane of Rava.
phrases.notes: This points to a known story: a man hid the coins he owed inside a hollow cane, handed it to the lender, then swore he had given him the money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from the court's warning in step 15.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof from the ברייתא, not רבינא's question itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The warning can be explained as protection against the cane trick, not as proof that private meanings count.

steps.title: Proof from משה's oath to ישראל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a new proof. משה told ישראל that they were swearing by God's meaning and his meaning, not their own. This seems to show he worried they would secretly mean an idol.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: When משה made ישראל swear, he told them: 'Know that I make you swear by God's meaning and my meaning, not by yours.' Why? He could have just said, 'Keep what God said!' Isn't it because they might have had an idol in mind?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries again to prove that private meaning matters in an oath. It uses משה's warning to ישראל. The next step answers this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word for 'God' could secretly mean an idol in someone's mind. משה added the warning to stop that, which suggests that without it, their private meaning would have counted. This would support רבינא's point about the flying camel.

keyTerms.meaning: According to the understanding of God

phrases.english: Come and hear: And so we found

phrases.aramaic: כְּשֶׁהִשְׁבִּיעַ מֹשֶׁה אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, אָמַר לָהֶן:
phrases.english: that when Moshe made Israel swear, he said to them:

phrases.aramaic: ״דְּעוּ שֶׁלֹּא עַל דַּעְתְּכֶם אֲנִי מַשְׁבִּיעַ אֶתְכֶם,
phrases.english: "Know that it is not by your understanding that I make you swear,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא עַל דַּעַת הַמָּקוֹם וְעַל דַּעְתִּי״.
phrases.english: but by the understanding of the Omnipresent and by my understanding."
And why? Let him say to them:
"Keep what God said"!
phrases.notes: The worry here is that someone could say 'God' out loud while privately having an idol in mind.

phrases.aramaic: לָאו מִשּׁוּם דְּמַסְּקִי אַדַּעְתַּיְיהוּ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה?
phrases.english: Is it not because they might have idol worship in mind?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the court proof was pushed away, the גמרא brings a new proof for the same idea.
steps.raayaObject: That the swearer's private meaning can change what an oath means.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא describing משה's warning when he made ישראל swear.

steps.title: The word 'God' itself can mean an idol
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof from משה. He added 'by God's meaning and mine' because the word 'אלוה' is unclear even in its plain meaning, not because of secret private meanings.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. The reason is that an idol is also called 'אלוה', as it is written: 'gods of silver and gods of gold.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof from step 17. It gives a different reason why משה spelled out whose meaning the oath followed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof assumed משה was worried about a private, secret meaning. The גמרא says the worry was simpler: the פסוק itself uses 'אלהי' for idols. So 'swear to keep God's word' is unclear even by its public meaning. That means the case proves nothing about private meanings.

keyTerms.meaning: God; the same word can also mean a god or idol

phrases.english: No;
because idol worship also
is called 'God,'
as it is written: 'gods of silver and gods of gold.'

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא; מִשּׁוּם דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה נָמֵי אִיקְּרִי אֱלוֹהַּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 17
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from משה's oath about private meanings
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ambiguity came from the word 'אלוה' itself, not from a secret private meaning

steps.title: Why not just say 'keep the Torah'?
steps.stepSummary: If the word 'God' was the problem, משה could have avoided it and simply said 'keep the Torah.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him say to them: 'Keep the Torah!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests a clearer wording משה could have used. This opens a series of 'why not say it this way?' questions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the word 'God' was unclear, why not leave it out and choose words that cannot be misread? 'Keep the Torah' sounds clear and complete.

phrases.english: But let him say to them:
'Keep the Torah!'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 18's claim that the word 'God' was the problem
steps.kashyaTarget: משה's choice of wording for the oath
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A clearer wording was available, so why use an unclear one and then add 'by my meaning'?

steps.title: That could mean only one Torah
steps.stepSummary: 'Torah' could be read as just one Torah, the Written or the Oral, and not both.
steps.simpleTranslation: That would be just one Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'keep the Torah' is also open to a narrow reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two Torahs, the Written and the Oral. The singular 'Torah' would let someone say he only swore to keep one of them.

phrases.english: That is one Torah.
phrases.notes: He means someone could say he only swore about the Written Torah or only about the Oral Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 19
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the proposed wording is also open to a narrow reading
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Torah' could mean only one of the two Torahs

steps.title: Then say 'keep two Torahs'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests saying 'two Torahs' to cover both the Written and the Oral.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him say: 'Keep two Torahs!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the last problem by suggesting a plural wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'Torah' might mean only one, then 'two Torahs' should clearly include both.

phrases.english: But let him say:
'Keep two Torahs!'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proposes a new wording to fix the problem in step 20

steps.title: 'Torah' can mean a single set of laws
steps.stepSummary: The word 'תורה' can also mean a narrow set of laws, like the laws of the חטאת or the אשם.
steps.simpleTranslation: That could mean 'the law of the sin-offering' and 'the law of the guilt-offering.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that 'two Torahs' could also be read narrowly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah itself uses 'תורת' for one specific set of rules, such as 'זאת תורת החטאת'. So someone could say he swore to keep just two such small sets of laws.

phrases.english: 'The law of the sin-offering,' 'the law of the guilt-offering.'
phrases.notes: The word 'Torah' can mean just one small group of rules, so 'two Torahs' could mean only these two.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 21
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the proposed wording is also open to a narrow reading
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Two Torahs' means the Written and the Oral
steps.terutzMaskana: It could mean two narrow sets of sacrifice laws

steps.title: Then say 'keep the entire Torah'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests 'the whole Torah,' which seems to leave no room for a narrow reading.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him say: 'Keep the entire Torah!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries an all-including wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'The entire Torah' should cover everything and block any limited reading.

phrases.english: 'Keep the entire Torah!'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proposes a new wording to fix the problem in step 22

steps.title: 'The entire Torah' could mean just the ban on idols
steps.stepSummary: Rejecting idols counts like keeping the whole Torah, so 'the entire Torah' could be read as only the ban on עבודה זרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: That could mean idol worship, as the Master said: Idol worship is so serious that anyone who rejects it is like someone who accepts the entire Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that even 'the entire Torah' has a narrow reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since a known teaching treats rejecting idols as equal to accepting the whole Torah, a person could claim he only swore to avoid idol worship. Ironically, that is the exact מצוה משה was worried about.

phrases.english: That means idol worship,
as the Master said:
Idol worship is severe,
so that anyone who rejects it
is like one who accepts the entire Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, דְּאָמַר מָר: חֲמוּרָה עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 23
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the proposed wording is also open to a narrow reading
steps.terutzMaskana: It could mean only the ban on idol worship, which counts like the whole Torah

steps.title: Then say 'keep the מצוה'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא moves from 'Torah' wording to 'מצוה' wording.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him say to them: 'Keep the מצוה!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a second round of suggested wordings, this time using the word 'מצוה'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since every 'Torah' wording had a loophole, maybe 'keep the מצוה' would be clearer.

phrases.english: But let him say to them:
'Keep the מצוה!'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries a new kind of wording after the 'Torah' wordings failed
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'מצוה' might avoid the problems of the word 'Torah'

steps.title: That is only one מצוה
steps.stepSummary: The singular 'מצוה' could mean just one commandment.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is one מצוה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the singular word is too narrow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone could claim he only swore to keep a single commandment.

phrases.english: That is one מצוה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 25
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the proposed wording is also open to a narrow reading

steps.title: Then say 'keep מצוות'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the plural 'מצוות'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him say: 'Keep מצוות!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the plural form.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plural should cover more than one commandment.

phrases.english: 'Keep מצוות!'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proposes a fix for step 26
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The plural avoids the 'only one' problem

steps.title: Plural could mean just two
steps.stepSummary: The plural 'מצוות' could be read as the smallest plural, just two.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is two.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that a plural can mean as few as two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The smallest number a plural can mean is two, so someone could say he swore to keep only two מצוות.

phrases.english: Two.
phrases.notes: A plural only has to mean at least two, so he could claim he swore about just two.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 27
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the proposed wording is also open to a narrow reading

steps.title: Then say 'all the מצוות'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests 'all the מצוות in their entirety.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him say: 'All the מצוות, every one of them!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the all-including form of 'מצוות'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'all' should block any limited count.

phrases.english: 'All the מצוות, every one of them!'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proposes a fix for step 28

steps.title: 'All the מצוות' could mean ציצית
steps.stepSummary: ציצית is said to equal all the מצוות, so 'all the מצוות' could be read as just ציצית.
steps.simpleTranslation: That could mean the מצוה of ציצית, as the Master said: The מצוה of ציצית is equal to all the מצוות together.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows a narrow reading again, this time using a teaching about ציצית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This follows the same pattern as idol worship in step 24. Since ציצית is said to weigh as much as all the מצוות, someone could claim 'all the מצוות' meant only ציצית.

phrases.english: That means the מצוה of ציצית,
as the Master said:
The מצוה of ציצית is equal
to all the מצוות together.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִצְוַת צִיצִית, דְּאָמַר מָר: שְׁקוּלָה מִצְוַת צִיצִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 29
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the proposed wording is also open to a narrow reading
steps.terutzMaskana: It could mean only ציצית, which equals them all

steps.title: Then say 'keep 613 מצוות'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests naming the exact number, 613, which seems impossible to read narrowly.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let him say to them: 'Keep 613 מצוות!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the most exact wording possible, a specific number.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A number cannot be shrunk the way the other wordings could. 613 means 613, so this seems to close every loophole.

phrases.english: But let him say to them:
'Keep 613 מצוות!'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֵימָא לְהוּ: קַיִּימוּ שֵׁשׁ מֵאוֹת וּשְׁלֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה מִצְוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Proposes a final, exact wording after all others had loopholes
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An exact number leaves no room for a narrow reading, so why didn't משה use it?

steps.title: By that logic, 'by my meaning' would be enough
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns the question around. If we keep asking for the best possible wording, we could also ask why משה said 'by God's meaning' when 'by my meaning' alone was enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: And by your reasoning, let him just say 'by my meaning.' Why do I need 'by God's meaning'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a 'by your own logic' reply. It shows that you can always ask why a different wording wasn't used, so the question has no force.
steps.deeperAnalysis: משה's 'by my meaning' already closed every loophole, so even his own words included something extra. That shows he simply chose a full, clear phrasing, so there is no point in asking why he didn't pick one specific other wording.
steps.whatToRemember: משה's wording was needed because 'אלוה' can also mean an idol, even in plain speech. Every other wording the גמרא suggests also has a narrow reading. Asking 'why not 613?' fails, because by that logic even 'by God's meaning' was more than needed.
steps.confusionAlert: The final line is not a new rule about oaths. It is a 'by your own logic' answer that shows the question proves too much.

phrases.english: And according to your reasoning,
let him say to them: 'By my meaning';
why do I need 'by God's meaning'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 31 by turning its logic around
steps.terutzResolutionType: A 'by your own logic' reply showing the question proves too much
steps.terutzHavaAmina: משה should have used the most exact wording, 613
steps.terutzMaskana: Even משה's own wording had more than needed, so there is no point asking why he didn't pick another wording
